scenes.title: SageMaker Data Wrangler
scenes.narration: Let's move from document extraction to visual preparation of tabular data. This slide shows the workflow in SageMaker Data Wrangler from left to right. First, import a dataset from an available source. Next, inspect and visualize it to discover missing values, unusual distributions, and inconsistent fields. In the middle is the transform stage, where we can filter rows, join datasets, clean strings, and generate features. The fourth step is a quick model that helps us assess whether the prepared data is useful for an initial machine-learning task. Finally, export the data flow so the transformations can be reused in a larger processing workflow, such as SageMaker Pipelines. Notice the note along the bottom: Data Wrangler is a preparation and exploration interface. It does not automatically build and deploy a production model merely because we created a visual data flow. In a real project, this distinction matters because data cleaning, model training, deployment, and ongoing monitoring are separate responsibilities. We want a repeatable, auditable preparation pipeline before relying on the model's output.

scenes.title: Data Wrangler Transforms
scenes.narration: This diagram begins with a small tabular dataset containing age, income, tenure, purchases, and a label. The orange transform box in the centre converts that raw data into a better-structured set of features. Look at the numbered transform examples along the bottom. The first balances classes, which may help when one label dominates the training examples. The second fills missing values, such as an absent income or age. The third handles outliers so extreme values do not unnecessarily distort the features. The fourth reduces dimensions to simplify the model input where appropriate. The final group shows additional operations, including image resizing and custom transformations using supported code or scripts. Notice the before-and-after table: the goal isn't to change values arbitrarily. Each transformation should address a documented data-quality issue and be fitted correctly within the training workflow, without leaking information from validation or test sets. When designing an AWS ML pipeline, ask which transforms need to run consistently during both training and inference.

scenes.title: Data Wrangler Sources and Destinations
scenes.narration: This slide clarifies where Data Wrangler sits in an end-to-end system. On the left are possible sources: Amazon S3, Athena, Redshift, SageMaker Feature Store, application datasets, and JDBC connections where supported. The arrows point into Data Wrangler's visual interface, which prepares and transforms data for machine-learning workflows. Now read the destination column on the right. Prepared output may be sent to SageMaker Processing, SageMaker Pipelines, SageMaker Feature Store, or exported for use in a notebook. Each destination has a different purpose. Feature Store is useful for managing features, while a pipeline coordinates repeatable processing or training steps. The orange note at the bottom warns that connectors are not all equivalent or automatic; some use IAM access and S3 staging, and others depend on configuration or current product support. A practical exam question might ask you to choose between connecting to a data source and scheduling reproducible processing. Treat ingestion, transformation, feature management, and orchestration as separate architectural decisions.

scenes.title: Import, Preview and Visualize
scenes.narration: Here is the first hands-on Data Wrangler workflow. The numbered boxes at the top take us through choosing a dataset source, previewing the rows and schema, and visualizing key attributes. Notice the customer-support dataset example with fields such as channel, issue type, priority, and resolution status. Before transforming anything, we should inspect missing values, unexpected categories, and outliers. On the right, visual charts show the distribution of case classes and missing data. This can reveal problems that are hard to spot by scanning a table of hundreds of records. The orange note at the bottom explains why these checks matter: data preparation decisions should be based on actual evidence. If a label is missing or heavily imbalanced, simply training a model may produce a misleading result. Once the dataset is understood, we can select transformations that address the problems identified. The sequence is important: import, inspect, visualize, and then transform. This makes data-cleaning work easier to explain, reproduce, and audit.

scenes.title: Transform, Quick Model and Export
scenes.narration: This slide continues the customer-support workflow. Start with the table on the left, which contains categorical fields such as channel, issue type, and priority, along with resolution status. The first stage applies transformations, including encoding categories, handling missing values, and preparing consistent numeric features. In the middle, the quick-model step tests whether the current features carry useful predictive signal. The example shows an initial model accuracy of seventy-eight percent. Treat this as a diagnostic result on the slide, not as a target or production guarantee. The next arrow leads to export. The data flow can become a repeatable processing job, pipeline step, or notebook workflow, depending on the selected output. The quality-check list at the bottom is the practical takeaway: inspect unexpected nulls, invalid categories, type mismatches, and feature changes before training. A quick model can reveal whether the current preparation is promising, but the full production process still needs proper training, evaluation, validation, deployment, and monitoring.

scenes.title: Data Wrangler Troubleshooting
scenes.narration: Our final Data Wrangler slide is a troubleshooting decision tree. Three common failures appear across the top. On the left is access denied when SageMaker Studio cannot open a notebook or Data Wrangler flow. Check the user's IAM or Studio authorization, the domain setup, and applicable permissions. In the middle is a source read failure. The tool may start correctly but cannot read the dataset in S3. Now inspect the role's S3 permissions, bucket policy, and encryption permissions if relevant. On the right is a compute quota or instance availability problem. Studio cannot start the compute needed for the session. Check instance type permissions, service quotas, and regional capacity rather than treating this as an S3 issue. The diagnostic boxes beneath each branch separate identity, data access, and compute capacity. This distinction will appear frequently in AWS troubleshooting scenarios: similar symptoms can originate in entirely different layers. We now have a repeatable way to transform tabular data. Next we'll move into AWS Glue for cataloging, ETL, and data quality.
